physical.title: Wall Hanging (pardah)
physical.medium_raw: Silk: warp-faced plain weave, warp-ikat; cotton weft
physical.summary: Dazzling patterns with saturated colors in the ikat technique provided vibrant wall hangings in reception rooms of the urban elite in Central Asia. In this splendid example composed of five loom widths, the three central lengths display a precise design of amulets complemented by palmettes in the two outer lengths. The irregular contours, telltale indicators of ikat, are masterfully controlled with five rich colors, illustrating the high quality of the earliest known examples in Central Asia from the first half of the 1800s. In the ikat technique, the design was dyed on the warp before it was woven in a resist-dye process. Thread was tightly wrapped around the warp to resist dye penetration for each area of color. This labor-intensive process created hangings and garments cherished for their vibrant colors with "fuzzy" contours.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a suzani embroidered textile with dense floral and foliate motifs, a well-documented Uzbek dowry craft tradition from Shakhrisyabz — a clear match to the claimed ethnicity.

physical.title: Suzani with floral sprays
physical.medium_raw: Cotton: plain weave, 6 strips; silk: embroidery; filling stitch: kanda xajol, occasionally bosma; outlining stitch: ilmoq
physical.summary:
Embroidered textiles were essential items in dowries. This type, known as a suzani after the Persian and Tajik word for needle, suzan, were created by mothers and daughters who proudly displayed them during wedding festivities and special occasions. This is an especially striking example, probably embroidered in Shakhrisyabz, located south of Samarkand in Uzbekistan, during 1800–1850.

Suzani were made for numerous functions including the nuptial bed, curtains for storage niches, and wrappers for various dry goods. Floral and foliate motifs generally dominate as seen here, enriched with several shades of red and enhanced by the varied light reflections and colors of the silk thread. Possibly the motifs conveyed cosmological, apotropaic, medicinal, or fertility associations especially for married life.

Patterns were drawn in black ink on several loosely joined cotton cloths by a skilled family member or a professional. The cloths were then separated, embroidered individually, and reattached, confirmed by mismatched motifs where the lengths are joined. They are generally attributed to nineteenth-century production after sericulture was introduced in the Merv area around 1800.

physical.title: Wall hanging (pardah)
physical.medium_raw: warp ikat, warp-faced plain weave; silk warp; cotton weft; 5 panels./ lining: printed cotton, plain weave; 2 panels
physical.summary: Eye-dazzling patterns with saturated colors demonstrating the ikat technique provided vibrant wall hangings for the reception rooms of the urban elite in Central Asia. In this splendid example comprising five loom widths, three lengths display popular amulet designs while the two inner lengths are precursors to the bold chevron designs of the late 19th century. The irregular contours—telltale indicators of ikat—are masterfully controlled with five rich colors. In the ikat technique, designs are dyed on the warp (vertical thread) in a resist-dye process before being woven. Thread is tightly wrapped around the warp to prevent dye penetration in each area of color, beginning with the lightest shades to the darkest. This labor-intensive process produces vivid colors and fuzzy contours.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a men's silk embroidered surcoat (khalat) from Shahr-i Sabz, Uzbekistan, a garment traditionally worn by Uzbeks; it matches the claimed ethnicity and origin.

physical.title: Man's surcoat (khalat)
physical.summary: Prestigious men’s surcoats embellished with designs such as this dramatic decoration in cross-stitch were among the most elaborate silk-thread embroidered garments in Central Asia. In a flamboyant style, large palmettes framed by split palmette leaves dominate with quartered rosettes and smaller flora on a brilliant yellow ground. Foliate vines enhance the edge along the front center opening, hemline, and cuffs. It is lined with an ikat of cypress trees and finger-looped trim. The style and technique represent professional work from Shahr-i Sabz, south of Samarkand. The pattern was drawn on the cotton ground cloth of the surcoat, then disassembled for stitching, and finally reassembled—revealed by severed and misaligned motifs plus mismatched colors.

raw.tombstone: Man's surcoat (khalat), late 1800s. Uzbekistan, Shahr-i Sabz. Silk: embroidery, cross-stitch; overall: 150 x 218.4 cm (59 1/16 x 86 in.). The Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Wade, 1916.1412

physical.title: Woman's cloak (chyrpy)
physical.summary:
This yellow silk is richly embroidered in the button-hole stitch. The pattern of this woman's cloak resembles one of the patterns on the so-called Bokhara stripes used for fixing tents.

The garment is lined with printed cotton fabric, which seems to be a product of India or Persia, and very crude block-printed cotton fabric with simple allover patterns of red and black dots and circular medallions.

physical.title: Wall Hanging
physical.medium_raw: Silk, cotton; plain weave, embroidery, tambour chain stitch
physical.summary: Embroideries known as suzani, after the Persian and Tajik word for needle (suzan), feature bold floral and foliate motifs enriched with several shades of red and crimson silk thread. This example suggests a lush garden enriched with single flowering plants alternating with a bird’s-eye view of blossoms in a foliate diamond trellis. Either a skilled family member or a professional drew the pattern in black ink (still visible) on five loosely joined cotton cloths; female family members disassembled them for stitching and reassembled them upon completion. Suzanis were made in many towns, generally with distinctive artistic and technical characteristics.

physical.title: shirt; adire; textile
physical.summary: Boy’s shirt (adire), made up from three pieces of imported European machine white calico cotton, indigo-dyed in Africa with a design drawn by hand in starch resist and then dyed in a single shade of indigo. The cotton was decorated with a repeated pattern of knots and flowers. One piece was cut to form the body with a circular hole cut for the head, and two pieces were cut to form the short sleeves; the whole was machine-sewn together. The neck of the garment has been lined with a piece of European printed cloth with an ikat design in maroon, black and white, and machine stitched with ornamental circles in white cotton; a small area at the bottom of the shirt has been lined with a white and blue European brocaded cotton.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a red twill scarf/shawl with dense polychrome embroidery (circular medallion, botehs, floral and hooked motifs) and fringe, consistent with Central Asian embroidered textiles of the Uzbek/Central Asian tradition (suzani-type work).

physical.title: scarf; shawl
physical.summary: A woman's scarf / shawl; square.  Ground made of red/pink twill woven cotton cloth, with two panels of the same fabric, each 9 cms deep, stitched to the bottom two sides.  Polychrome embroidery in lower half of scarf: a large circular motif framed by four large botehs (two different colourways). Circular motif is divided into eight segments - each containing a floral motif - with the same colours opposite: black/orange; orange/blue; pink/green.  Edge of circle has green 'hooked' motifs; further floral and 'hooked' motifs fill out the centre ground.  Line of blue curvilinear designs across widest part of scarf.  White cotton rick rack divides the main ground from the panels, which contain cross stitch embroidery: geometric patterning worked in four different colourways.  A green passementerie trimming stitched to edge (finger braiding?) with plied fringing joined at the bottom and threaded with small white plastic (?) beads.  Panels lined with three different printed cotton cloths (cream/pink): 6 pieces in total.
